title: How to Make a Budget That Honors God
excerpt: A budget is a moral document. It records what you actually love, not what you say you love. Here is how to build one that tells the truth and then bends toward God.
body:
A budget is not a math problem. It is a confession. Show me where your money went last month and I will show you what you worship, no matter what came out of your mouth on Sunday. Jesus said it plainly: where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. He did not say your heart leads your treasure. He said your treasure reveals your heart, and often drags it along behind.

So making a budget that honors God starts with being willing to read the confession your spending has already written.

## First, look at what is already true

Before you plan a single dollar, account for the last sixty days. Pull every transaction. Put it in categories. Do not flinch.

Most people skip this because it is humiliating. You discover you spent more on takeout than on giving, more on subscriptions you forgot than on anyone outside your own household. I have done this exercise and wanted to close the laptop and pretend I never saw it.

Don't close the laptop. This is the work. You cannot honor God with a fantasy of who you wish you were. You can only honor him with the actual person whose actual money did actual things. The budget is the place where that person gets handed over to be changed.

## Give first, off the top

The order matters more than the amount. Scripture's pattern is firstfruits, the first and best, not the leftovers. "Honor the Lord with your wealth, with the firstfruits of all your crops," says Proverbs. Israel did not give God what survived the month. They gave first, before they knew whether the rest would be enough.

So generosity is line one, not the line you reach if anything remains. Decide the number before the month begins and move it the day you are paid. This is not because God needs your money. It is because giving first breaks money's claim to be first. You are reminding your own heart, every single month, who actually owns you.

Start somewhere honest even if it is small. A real five percent given off the top forms you more than a guilty ten percent you never quite manage.

## Provide before you indulge

The next claim on the budget is provision. "If anyone does not provide for his relatives, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith," Paul writes, in language so severe it should stop us. Housing, food, the bills that keep the lights on and the family fed and the debts current. This is not the boring part of a holy budget. This is holy.

Provision also includes the future. A margin for the car that will break, the roof that will leak, the income that may stop. Proverbs sends the sluggard to watch the ant, who stores in summer for the winter it cannot yet see. Saving is not faithlessness. It is the ant's quiet wisdom, refusing to make tomorrow's emergency into someone else's crisis.

## Name your indulgences and keep them

Here is what many religious budgets get wrong. They are built to fail, all denial and no joy, a spreadsheet shaped like a frown. That budget gets abandoned by the fifteenth, and then guilt does the rest.

God is not against your enjoyment. Paul tells Timothy that God "richly provides us with everything to enjoy." A faithful budget has a line for delight, named out loud, given a number, and then spent without shame. The discipline is not in having no pleasures. It is in deciding them in advance instead of letting them leak out of you in a hundred unaccounted purchases.

A budget with no joy in it does not honor God. It just makes him sound stingy, which he is not.

## Build it where two people can see it

If you are married, the budget is not yours. Money secrecy is a slow poison, and the budget is the antidote, the one document where everything is on the table and you both signed it. If a category cannot survive your spouse seeing it, the problem is not the budget. The problem is the category.

## This week

Do the sixty-day look-back. One sitting, every transaction, sorted into categories, no flinching. Then write four numbers for next month before it starts: give, provide, save, enjoy, in that order. Move the giving number the day your pay lands, before anything else can lay a claim on it.

You will not get the numbers right the first time. That is fine. The budget is not a cage you build once and live in. It is a confession you make every month, and slowly, dollar by dollar, it becomes true.
